The statement was more a "water is wet" type of statement, to me. Worse, a bit smug - but not all articles are exceptional, some are just acceptable. In that case, we know water is wet - but that doesn't really increase our knowledge. I think, in this case, they are trying too hard to make it simple. It's not a terrible effort and a laudable goal.

There is a kind of neural network which has layers but isn't as organizationally layered as a back-propagation network. Because of that they are called sparse. Any node can have as an input a node higher than itself (maybe there are convolutional ones). Nodes fire off randomly but their frequency depends on how recently they have recieved impuses from upstream nodes. They don't actually spit out a result like a back-propagation network but instead perform impulses.

These are usually tied to genetic algorithms and there is a performance metric such as survival time or how much of an action was done in a certain time. Ones that perform less well are killed and ones that perform better reproduce and have mutations. The advantage beside being more applicable to impulse and actions is that no training data is needed. A human doesn't need to classify outputs and train a NN to copy. Because of this they can outperform humans and solve problems where a human doesn't want to understand the problem but rather have a machine figure it out.

In theory you could give it zero inputs and have it run blind, but it is most definately not just a regression or a 1:1 input/output machine.
